entries.sentence: The symptoms of an overactive thyroid can appear gradually or suddenly, and they vary in how severe they are.
entries.note: NHS symptoms page: symptoms can appear gradually or suddenly and vary in severity.

entries.sentence: People often notice nervousness, irritability, mood swings, poor sleep and persistent tiredness.
entries.note: NHS overview symptom list: nervousness, irritability, mood swings, trouble sleeping, tiredness.

entries.sentence: Other common changes include sensitivity to heat, a fast or irregular heartbeat, a tremor and weight loss.
entries.note: NHS overview list: heat sensitivity, fast or irregular heartbeat, tremor, weight loss.

entries.sentence: Some people also have a visibly enlarged thyroid, called a goitre.
entries.note: NHS overview lists goitre.

entries.sentence: Because many of these symptoms are the same as in other conditions, symptoms alone cannot confirm the diagnosis.
entries.note: NIDDK: diagnosis cannot be based on symptoms alone because many are shared with other diseases.

entries.sentence: In older adults the picture can look different, with loss of appetite or withdrawal rather than restlessness.
entries.note: NIDDK: older adults may show appetite loss or withdrawal.

entries.sentence: For this reason the condition is sometimes mistaken for depression or dementia in older people.
entries.note: NIDDK: sometimes mistaken for depression or dementia.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP if you have symptoms of an overactive thyroid.
entries.note: NHS and NHS 111 Wales: see a GP if you have symptoms; blood test is the usual first step.

entries.sentence: A blood test of thyroid function is the usual first step.
entries.note: NHS 111 Wales summary: thyroid function blood test is the usual first step.

entries.sentence: The most common cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition.
entries.note: NHS overview and MedlinePlus: Graves' disease is the most common cause.

entries.sentence: NHS pages put its share at roughly 3 in 4 to 4 in 5 cases, depending on the page.
entries.note: NHS overview about 4 in 5; NHS 111 Wales about 3 in 4.

entries.sentence: Other causes include thyroid nodules, inflammation of the gland called thyroiditis, and medicines such as amiodarone.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS pages: nodules, thyroiditis, amiodarone.

entries.sentence: Iodine supplements can also trigger it in some people, usually those who already have thyroid nodules.
entries.note: NHS inform summary: iodine supplements can trigger it, usually in people with nodules.

entries.sentence: A single overactive nodule, called a toxic adenoma, is another cause.
entries.note: Search summary of MedlinePlus/other: toxic adenoma is a single overactive nodule; page attribution not certain.

entries.sentence: Further tests can help to tell the causes apart.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis pages: other tests and scans may be needed; antibody test helps identify Graves'.

entries.sentence: An antibody blood test can help identify Graves' disease.
entries.note: NHS 111 Wales: antibody test can help identify Graves' disease.

entries.sentence: A radioactive iodine uptake test can also help, with high uptake typical of Graves' disease and low uptake typical of thyroiditis.
entries.note: Search summary: RAIU used to differentiate causes; high uptake Graves, low thyroiditis; page attribution to MedlinePlus likely, not certain.

entries.sentence: The starting point is a visit to a GP, who can arrange a thyroid function blood test.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis page: see a GP; blood test.

entries.sentence: A thyroid function blood test is the main method used to diagnose it.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis summary: thyroid function test is the main method.

entries.sentence: This test measures thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and the thyroid hormones T3 and T4.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis: measures TSH, T3 and T4.

entries.sentence: A low TSH with a high T3 or T4 usually points to an overactive thyroid.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis summary: low TSH with high T3/T4 usually points to overactive thyroid.

entries.sentence: Other blood tests and a scan may also be needed, and NHS Scotland mentions an isotope thyroid scan.
entries.note: Search summary: other tests and scan may be needed; NHS Scotland notes isotope scan.

entries.sentence: Once the diagnosis is made, a GP usually refers the person to an endocrinologist, a specialist in hormone conditions, who plans the treatment.
entries.note: NHS Scotland and NHS 111 Wales: referral to endocrinologist to plan treatment.

entries.sentence: A mild form, called subclinical, may not need treatment but needs repeat thyroid function tests to keep an eye on it.
entries.note: NHS Scotland: mild form may not need treatment but repeat tests; NHS treatment: some people with subclinical need no treatment.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes three main treatments: medicine, radioactive iodine treatment and surgery.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Antithyroid medicines such as carbimazole or propylthiouracil are the usual first step.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: They are usually taken for 12 to 18 months, and it may be a few months before any benefit is noticed.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Some people need to continue the medicine for several years or possibly for life.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Beta-blockers can relieve some symptoms, but they are not suitable for people with asthma.
entries.note: NHS treatment page: beta-blockers such as propranolol relieve symptoms; not suitable for asthma.

entries.sentence: Radioactive iodine is a highly effective treatment, and most people need only one treatment.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: It is not suitable for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, or for people with severe eye problems caused by the condition.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Surgery is used only occasionally, for example for a large goitre, severe eye problems, when other treatments cannot be used, or when symptoms return after other treatment.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid, which is sometimes temporary but often permanent and needs long-term thyroid hormone medicine.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: Surgery to remove the thyroid also usually leads to lifelong hormone replacement.
entries.note: NHS complications/treatment pages: lifelong thyroid hormone tablets after surgery.

entries.sentence: Eye problems, known as thyroid eye disease or Graves' ophthalmopathy, can occur in people whose overactive thyroid is caused by Graves' disease.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: NHS pages give different figures, from around 1 in 20 to around 1 in 4 people with Graves' disease.
entries.note: Search summaries: one NHS page 1 in 20, another about 1 in 4.

entries.sentence: Symptoms can include dryness, bulging eyes and double vision.
entries.note: NHS symptoms page: dryness, double vision, bulging eyes.

entries.sentence: Many people have mild eye symptoms, and these often improve once the overactive thyroid is controlled.
entries.note: NHS complications summary.

entries.sentence: Severe eye disease can threaten vision, and treatment may include eye drops, steroids or surgery.
entries.note: NHS complications summary: vision loss possible; eye drops, steroids, surgery.

entries.sentence: Smoking increases the risk of eye problems and is linked with more severe eye changes.
entries.note: MedlinePlus summary: smoking increases risk and severity of eye abnormalities.

entries.sentence: Thyroid UK says eye problems can continue in people who keep smoking after their thyroid is treated.
entries.note: Thyroid UK summary.

entries.sentence: If your sight changes suddenly or your eyes become painful, contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day.
entries.note: Route-to-care sentence; consistent with the page's seekCare field, not from returned text.

entries.sentence: Pregnant women with an overactive thyroid are at increased risk of complications in pregnancy and birth, such as miscarriage and eclampsia.
entries.note: NHS complications page summary.

entries.sentence: NIDDK says mild hyperthyroidism in pregnancy is usually not a problem, but severe disease that is not treated can affect both the mother and the baby.
entries.note: NIDDK summary.

entries.sentence: Pregnant women need specialist management, typically with a medicine that does not harm the baby.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary.

entries.sentence: Radioactive iodine is not suitable during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Reviews stress that early diagnosis and keeping thyroid hormone levels controlled are key to lowering the risk of complications for the mother and the baby.
entries.note: Review summary: early diagnosis and controlled levels reduce maternal, fetal and newborn complications.

entries.sentence: A clinical review describes monitoring of thyroid function and thyroid antibodies, with checks on the baby, as the mainstay of care for Graves' disease in pregnancy.
entries.note: Review PMC5831855 summary: TRAb measurement, thyroid function monitoring and fetal surveillance.

entries.sentence: An overactive thyroid is usually treatable, according to the NHS.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: If it is not controlled, it can raise the chance of atrial fibrillation, an irregular and often abnormally fast heart rhythm, as well as heart failure and weakened bones.
entries.note: NHS complications summary: AF, heart failure, osteoporosis.

entries.sentence: Rarely, an undiagnosed or poorly controlled overactive thyroid can lead to thyroid storm, a serious, life-threatening condition.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists triggers such as infection, pregnancy, not taking medicine correctly and injury to the thyroid.
entries.note: NHS complications summary.

entries.sentence: Warning signs include a rapid heartbeat, high temperature, confusion and loss of consciousness.
entries.note: NHS complications and NHS 111 Wales.

entries.sentence: Severe thyroid eye disease can lead to vision loss, and radioactive iodine or surgery can leave the thyroid underactive.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: Thyroid storm is an emergency, and anyone with these signs needs 999.
entries.note: Route-to-care sentence; not from returned text.

entries.sentence: A mild form, called subclinical, may not need treatment, though it needs repeat thyroid function tests.
entries.note: NHS Scotland and NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Other people are treated with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Some need medicine for several years or possibly for life.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: A GP can arrange the thyroid blood test that starts the process.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis page.

entries.sentence: No, an overactive thyroid makes too much thyroid hormone, while an underactive thyroid means hormone levels are too low.
entries.note: NHS overview (gland makes too much hormone); NHS complications (levels too low).

entries.sentence: Treatment for an overactive thyroid, such as radioactive iodine or surgery, can lead to an underactive thyroid.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: This then needs long-term thyroid hormone medicine.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: Thyroid storm is rare but life-threatening, and can occur when an overactive thyroid is undiagnosed or poorly controlled.
entries.note: NHS complications page.

entries.sentence: Its signs include a rapid heartbeat, high temperature, confusion and loss of consciousness.
entries.note: NHS complications and NHS 111 Wales.

entries.sentence: Anyone with these signs needs an emergency response, so call 999.
entries.note: Route-to-care sentence; not from returned text.

entries.sentence: The NHS says radioactive iodine is not suitable for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: It is also not suitable for people with severe eye problems caused by the condition.
entries.note: NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Surgery is an option in some of these situations, such as severe eye problems.
entries.note: NHS treatment page lists severe eye problems among reasons for surgery.

entries.sentence: The specialist team advises which treatment fits each person.
entries.note: NHS Scotland and NHS 111 Wales: endocrinologist plans treatment.

entries.sentence: Yes, many of its symptoms are shared with other conditions, so symptoms alone cannot confirm it.
entries.note: NIDDK summary.

entries.sentence: In older adults it is sometimes mistaken for depression or dementia.
entries.note: NIDDK summary.

entries.note: NHS symptoms page.

entries.sentence: A thyroid function blood test helps to sort this out.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis page.

entries.note: NHS overview names it hyperthyroidism, also called thyrotoxicosis.

entries.note: NHS overview/MedlinePlus.

entries.note: NHS diagnosis page.

entries.note: NHS treatment page.
